entry.title: Was Trigonometry Really About Triangles?
entry.content:
1. Introduction

Recently I’ve been teaching a student the fundamentals of trigonometry. Naturally, I started with introducing sine, cosine, and tangent as ratios of the sides of a right triangle. But as I was doing so, I realized that I had no clue why anyone would think to make those ratios in the first place, and that left me very unsatisfied. It’s not really necessary to know these things if you just want to know the math, but it’s not very interesting for the learner if it’s just like, well here’s a thing and you can do some things with it and it’s magic basically…. So I like to make up some stories that motivate the math, and although I say “make up”, they’re usually based on history. It’s just that I don’t really care about being super accurate if it doesn’t make the math feel any more motivated.

I should quickly mention that I will be assuming some level of geometric knowledge, though only basic knowledge that I didn’t bother proving when I was researching. At most, I will assume that you know what similar and congruent triangles are and how to tell when triangles are similar or congruent. I will also assume the Pythagorean Theorem.

With that said, let’s start investigating the origins of the trigonometric functions that we use so much today.

2. Ancient Greek and Roman Astronomy

The origins of the sine function start with the Ancient Greeks in the form of the chord function. A chord is a line segment with endpoints on a circle. We can associate a central angle of the circle by drawing two radii from the center to the endpoints of the chord. Since this central angle also specifies an arc of the same degree, we can also associate a chord with the arc defined by the chord’s endpoints.

A chord in orange and its corresponding arc in purple at various angles up to 180 degrees.

This correspondence between angles (or arcs) and chords (specifically, the lengths of chords) defines the chord function. We will denote this by \(\crd{\theta}\), where \(\theta\) is the central angle corresponding to the chord. While the Greeks would’ve used the degree of an arc instead of the central angle, the formulations are equivalent, so I’m just going to use central angles to make it more familiar. The Greeks did not define the chord function for angles over 180 degrees, presumably because it wasn’t necessary and there wasn’t a natural way to do so.

The Greek astronomer Hipparchus of Rhodes is credited with the making the earliest known chord table. Unfortunately, most of his work has been lost, and the only reason we even know about his chord table is because Claudius Ptolemy referenced it in his Almagest, a huge textbook containing all the astronomical knowledge obtained up until that point. Ptolemy improved on Hipparchus’s chord table by finding the chord lengths for angles in half-degree increments up to 180 degrees, whereas Hipparchus’s table had increments of 7.5 degrees.

To understand how they used the chord function in astronomy, let’s look at a problem on page 7-9 from G.J. Toomer’s translation of the Almagest, which is what he calls a “typical calculation involving trigonometry”. I won’t be covering the actual context in which the problem appears because it’s very involved. Instead, I’ll make up my own context which seems plausible enough to me.

The Retrograde Motion of Mars

The apparent retrograde motion of Mars. GIF by Eugene Alvin Villar (seav), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Mars (and other objects) are subject to a strange phenomenon where they occasionally appear to move move backwards in the sky. This is called apparent retrograde motion.

We know now that the Earth revolves around the Sun along with the other planets. Since Mars takes slightly less than twice as long as Earth to complete its orbit, it completes about a quarter of its orbit in the same time that it takes Earth to complete half its orbit. If Mars is at the right position in its orbit, Earth will then pass it by since Earth completes its orbit faster. This makes it look like Mars is lagging behind in the sky. Earth kind of “slows down” at some point because it needs to follow its curved orbit, and Mars is able to catch up and resumes its normal motion in the sky. See the animation for a better idea of what this looks like.

However, the Ancient Greeks did not believe in heliocentrism, and tried to adapt the geocentric model to explain this phenomenon. The theory they came up with was that Mars was actually on a small orbit called an epicycle, which itself revolved around the Earth in an orbit called the deferent. Ptolemy improved on this model and formalized it in the Almagest. This did explain the retrograde motion of the planets, but it also eventually became pretty insane and hard to work with. Reducing the number of epicycles was one of the advantages of the Copernican heliocentric model, although apparently he eventually added a bunch of epicycles anyway. Even so, the Ptolemaic model was very accurate at predicting the locations of planets since any orbit shape can be traced out by adding more and more epicycles (essentially a Fourier series).

The theory of epicycles explains Mars's backwards motion by putting it on a secondary orbit. Heliocentrism explains the phenomenon using changes in viewing angle from Earth. The red line being traced by the dashed line is how we would see the location of Mars from Earth.

If you were an astronomer, something you might want to do is predict where Mars will be in the sky at some time. More specifically, you want to predict how far Mars will lag behind in the sky due to its epicyclic motion. You would know from the model the location of Mars and its epicycle, and what you want to know is the difference in angle between the expected position \(C\) (the center of the epicycle) and the actual position \(M\). Suppose at this time, Mars will be 30 degrees to the right of the line \(EC\), where point \(E\) is the Earth.

We know that \(EC = 60\), \(CM = 2.5\) (marked in green) and \(\angle{ECM} = 30^\circ\). Note that the length of \(EC\) is arbitrarily chosen to be 60 because it doesn’t matter for our angle calculations as long as everything is scaled accordingly. The number 60 comes from the Babylonians, who used base 60 instead of base 10 like we do. Hipparchus started using circles with radius 60 when he made his chord table, and this became the convention for a long time afterwards.

Math is something where you only really understand things after getting your hands dirty (figuratively), so I’m going to make this calculation an exercise. I’ll write up the full solution at the end, but I recommend you try to do it yourself; it’s fun!

Exercise 1

Objective: Find \(\angle{CEM}\).

Hint: In every step, you should try to involve similar triangles somehow. The information gathered from similarity will help you a lot.

  1. Drop an altitude from \(M\) to \(EC\). Call the point of intersection \(K\). Note that \(KM\) is perpendicular to \(EC\) by definition.
  2. Show that we can construct a circle with diameter \(CM\) that goes through \(K\) in the following way:
    1. Let \(O\) be the midpoint of \(CM\).
    2. Show that \(KO\) is equal to \(CO\) and \(OM\).
    3. Conclude that \(K\) is on the circle with diameter \(CM\).
  3. Use the fact that, for a circle with radius 60,
    \(\crd{60^\circ} = 60\) to find the length of \(KM\).
  4. Find the length of \(EM\) (use the Pythagorean Theorem).
  5. Use the result proven in (2) to construct a circle with diameter \(EM\) that goes through \(K\).
  6. Use the fact that, for a circle with radius 60, \(\crd{2.47^\circ} = 2.594\) find the central angle corresponding to the chord \(KM\) of >the circle constructed in (5).
  7. Show that \(\angle{KEM}\) (which is the same angle as \(\angle{CEM}\)) is exactly half of the angle calculated in (6).

4. The Half-Chord

Jyā, shown in solid orange and koti-jyā, shown in solid grey. The dashed lines show that both are half a chord. The corresponding arcs are colored purple and blue respectively.

At some point, the Greek and Roman idea of chords made its way to India, where a chord was called jyā, which also meant bowstring. They must have decided later that the ardha-jyā, or half-chord was more useful, as the mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata created a table of half-chords in his work, the Aryabhatiya. Eventually, the term jyā was used to refer to the half-chord for simplicity, presumably because no one ever used full chords. They also gave a name to the half-chord of the complementary angle, calling it koti-jyā.

If you worked through the exercise in the previous section, you may have noticed that using chords is pretty terrible, since we never actually wanted to use full chords or the angles associated with them. Instead, we wanted to know the length of half the chord and the angle associated with half the chord. So it seems fairly natural to move towards using a half-chord function instead of the chord function.

The jyā function later was translated to Arabic as jība, and when the function got back to Europe, it was misinterpreted as jaib, meaning something like “breast pocket”, since they are written the same way in Arabic. So it was translated to sinus in Latin, meaning the same thing, which became English “sine”. Since koti-jyā was the sine of the complement angle, it became complementi sinus, and from there became “cosine”.

It’s important to note that at this time, sine was the length of the half-chord, which depends on the radius of the circle, rather than the unitless ratios of today. I will capitalize the function (i.e. Sine) if it refers to a length from now on to differentiate it from the modern definition.

5. Telling Time with Shadows

In the medieval Islamic world, being able to tell the time precisely was a big deal because their religion required them to pray at certain times of the day. To tell the time, they used an instrument called a gnomon, which is the part of a sundial that casts a shadow. In it’s simplest form, it’s just a vertical stick in the ground. Then to go from the length of the shadow to the time of day, they utilized the Sine function, which had made its way over to the Middle East from India. Their techniques are recorded in The Exhaustive Treatise on Shadows by Iranian Khwarazmian polymath Abu Reyhan Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Biruni.

Al-Biruni defined two types of shadows: the direct shadow and the reverse shadow. The direct shadow is a shadow cast by a vertical gnomon in the ground, while the reverse shadow is the shadow cast below a horizontal gnomon on the wall. Suppose that we had a gnomon casting a direct shadow. How could we use that to tell the time? First, some setup. Imagine you are the gnomon. Point towards the Sun and draw a circle going directly overhead. Then the Sun and the direct shadow are in the same plane as the circle. This circle is called a circle of altitude.

We want to know the angle between the horizon plane and the Sun’s direction. Because we are only looking for the angle, it doesn’t actually matter what the radius of the circle of altitude is. For simplicity, I take the radius of the circle of altitude to be the same length as the gnomon. You will also notice that I center the circle of altitude on the top of the gnomon in the figure and not the ground. That should make sense, because the top of the gnomon determines where the shadow is cast. Therefore, the horizon plane is the horizontal axis of the circle of altitude, and when the Sun reaches this plane the shadow cast is infinitely long. Now, let’s actually figure out how to calculate the angle between the Sun and the horizon.

$$DE$$ is direct shadow cast by the gnomon $$CD$$.

Exercise 2

Objective: Find \(\angle{ACB}\) using the measurable quantities \(CD\) and \(DE\).

  1. Show that \(\triangle{ABC}\) and \(\triangle{CDE}\) are similar.
  2. Find the length of \(AB\).
  3. Justify to yourself that with the appropriate Sine table, knowing the length of \(AB\) and the length of \(CD\) is enough to determine \(\angle{ACB}\).

With this, we have obtained, for a particular gnomon length, a procedure to find the angle between the horizon plane and the Sun (which tells us the time of day) from the length of the direct shadow cast by the gnomon. Notice that we can also reverse the process and find the length of the direct shadow based on the angle between the horizon plane and the Sun. Hence one could pre-calculate the length of the shadow for various angles and produce a table of shadow lengths for a quick reference when trying to tell the time.

Since I made the radius of the circle of altitude the same length as the gnomon, you may notice that the shadow is tangent to the circle of altitude, i.e. it touches the circle at exactly one point (tangent comes from Latin tangere, meaning “to touch”). Because of this, you might think that the length of the direct shadow would be called the “Tangent” of the angle between the horizon and the Sun (capital “T” since it depends on the radius of the circle). However, because the angle that directly defines the length of the shadow is the angle between the gnomon and the line of sunlight, i.e. \(\angle{DCE}\), it’s more accurate to call it the “Tangent of the complementary angle”, or Cotangent.

We can also give a name to the length of \(CE\), the shadow’s “hypotenuse”. Since it’s part of the line of sunlight cutting through the circle, we call it the Cosecant, where “secant” comes from Latin secare, meaning “to cut”. The reason for the “co-“ prefix is the same as Cotangent.

For the reverse shadow, we can construct at the following figure in a similar way to the direct shadow:

$$DE$$ is reverse shadow cast by the gnomon $$CD$$.

We can once again find the angle between the horizon plane and the Sun using the length of the shadow. This isn’t worth making into an exercise, but you should convince yourself that this can be done.

Once again, the shadow is tangent to the circle of altitude. However, this time the angle which defines the shadow is equal to the angle between the horizon plane and the Sun. So it makes sense to simply call this the Tangent. We can also call the length of \(CE\) Secant for the same reason.

By the 10th century, all six modern trigonometric functions were used. However, they were not yet thought of in terms of right triangles.

Generalization

With all six trigonometric functions defined, let’s turn to the problem of generalization. Currently, there’s a lot of baggage associated with our functions which makes them hard to use outside of the context they were originally defined in. For instance, to use the Sine function, you would have to construct the appropriately sized circle for “half-chord” to make any sense. This is not very convenient because, if you recall from Exercise 1 with the chord function, typically we don’t really use the circle for anything other than justifying our usage of the function. It would be better if we could come up with an alternate characterization that needs the least amount of context possible.

A common way to do this in math is to base our definitions on properties we want to have. For example, applying the Pythagorean Theorem to \(\triangle{CDE}\) in the figure of the reverse shadow gives us that, for a specified gnomon length (radius) \(r\), \(r^2 + \operatorname{Tan^2}{\theta} = \operatorname{Sec^2}{\theta}\). Then, if we have a right triangle with an interior angle of \(\theta\) and the leg adjacent to \(\theta\) is length \(r\), then this triangle is congruent to \(\triangle{CDE}\) by the ASA congruence theorem. To satisfy the Pythagorean identity above, the other leg must be length \(\operatorname{Tan}{\theta}\) and the hypotenuse must be length \(\operatorname{Sec}{\theta}\). In this way, the constraint imposed by this Pythagorean identity completely determines the values of \(\operatorname{Tan}{\theta}\) and \(\operatorname{Sec}{\theta}\). This means that we can use this condition equivalently to the original definition of the two functions.

The definition of \(\operatorname{Tan}{\theta}\) would then look like:

Definition: Suppose we have a right triangle with an interior angle \(\theta\) such that the length of the leg adjacent to \(\theta\) has length \(r\). Then we call the length of the leg opposite to \(\theta\) the Tangent of \(\theta\).

We can redefine the other functions similarly for a specified radius \(r\) by using the Pythagorean identities \(\operatorname{Sin^2}{\theta} + \operatorname{Cos^2}{\theta} = r^2\) and \(\operatorname{Cot^2}{\theta} + r^2 = \operatorname{Csc^2}{\theta}\). For Sine and Cosine, we didn’t directly involve right triangles originally, but it should be trivial to prove that the Pythagorean identity is true.

So Where Do Ratios Come In?

At this point, we’re still defining the trigonometric functions in terms of length. So why did they come to represent ratios? I couldn’t find that much information about this, but it seems to naturally come from using \(r=1\) to calculate trigonometric tables. Let’s see how this could be the case.

Looking back at Exercise 1 again, something annoying we had to deal with was that the chord table was calculated for a circle of radius 60. This made it so that in Step 3 we had to scale down the result from the chord table by the appropriate factor, which we had to do an extra calculation to find. To simplify things, we could instead calculate chord tables using radius 1, which makes the scaling factor equal to the radius of our circle (this can be shown easily using the properties of similar triangles).

In Step 6, we wanted to find the central angle corresponding to the chord \(KM\). To do this, we had to scale up our circle by the appropriate scaling factor to obtain a circle of radius 60 so that we could use the chord table. With a chord table calculated for a radius of 1, we would instead simply divide the length of \(KM\) by the radius of the circle to find the right length to reference the chord table with, i.e. we would use the entry which says \(\crd{2.47^\circ} = \frac{KM}{EM/2}\). It’s not hard to see how \(\crd{}\) could come to be seen as a unitless ratio of lengths instead of a (unitful?) length itself once we start using chord tables calculated for radius 1.

Similarly, if we start using trigonometric tables calculated for “radius 1” (technically there isn’t a radius anymore but you know what I mean), it’s easy to see why they would end up being seen as ratios. Using lowercase notation to represent ratios, we obtain the following presentation.

The side lengths of these three triangles define the six trigonometric functions.

Since the figure doesn’t explicitly display units, these side lengths are really “\(\sin{\theta}\) units”, where
\(\sin{\theta} = \frac{(\sin{\theta})\text{ units}}{1\text{ unit}}\).

entry.title: The Change-of-Basis Matrix
entry.content:
1. Introduction

I recently came across a linear algebra problem about change of basis, which went something like this:

Problem: Let \(B_{old} = \left(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right),\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\right)\) and \(B_{new} = \left(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right),\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\right)\) be bases for \(\R^2\). Find the change-of-basis matrix from \(B_{old}\) to \(B_{new}\).

To be completely honest, I kinda forgot what the change-of-basis matrix was supposed to look like (I’m pretty rusty on my linear algebra). I didn’t want to just look it up though, so I tried to figure it out. My thought process went as follows:

Solution(?): Changing basis means that if I have some vector expressed in terms of \(B_{old}\), then I want to figure out how that same vector would be expressed in terms of \(B_{new}\). What exactly does it mean to express a vector in terms of a basis? Well, every vector has a unique representation as a linear combination of basis vectors. Let’s first label the basis vectors of \(B_{old}\) as \(\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2\) and label the basis vectors of \(B_{new}\) as \(\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\). So in more precise terms, changing basis would mean that if we have a arbitrary vector \(\mathbf{w}\) which is represented in terms of the old basis as \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), i.e. \(\mathbf{w}=a\mathbf{u}_1+b\mathbf{u}_2\), then I want to translate it into a linear combination of \(\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\) to get the representation of the same object in the new basis.

So how can I do that? Well, I thought that since \(\mathbf{w}\) is a linear combination of \(\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2\), then I should first figure out what \(\vec{u}_1,\vec{u}_2\) are as linear combinations of \(\vec{v}_1,\vec{v}_2\), since if \(\vec{u}_1 = c_1\vec{v}_1 + c_2\vec{v}_2\) and
\(\vec{u}_2 = d_1\vec{v}_1+d_2\vec{v}_2\), then

\[\begin{aligned} \vec{w} &= a\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2 \\ &= a(c_1\vec{v}_1+c_2\vec{v}_2)+b(d_1\vec{v}_1+d_2\vec{v}_2) \\ &= (ac_1+bd_1)\vec{v}_1+(ac_2+bd_2)\vec{v}_2 \end{aligned}\]

In other words, \(\vec{w}\) is represented as \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) in the old basis, and in the new basis this becomes \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}ac_1+bd_1\\ ac_2+bc_2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\).

So now the task has turned into figuring out what the \(c_i\) and \(d_i\) are supposed to be. Writing
\(\vec{u}_1=c_1\vec{v}_1+c_2\vec{v}_2\) out in terms of the concrete vectors gives us

\[\begin{aligned} \left(\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}\right) &= c_1\left(\begin{matrix}-1\\1\end{matrix}\right) + c_2\left(\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right) \\ &= \left(\begin{matrix}-c_1\\ c_1+c_2\end{matrix}\right) \\ &= \left(\begin{matrix}-1&0\\1&1\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}c_1\\ c_2\end{matrix}\right) \end{aligned}\]

Now we can just solve for \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}c_1\\ c_2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) using basic linear algebra techniques to find that \(c_1=-1\) and \(c_2=1\). A similar argument shows that \(d_1=-1\) and \(d_2=2\).

Putting everything together, we have that \(\vec{w} = (-a-b)\vec{v}_1+(a+2b)\vec{v}_2\), giving us the representation of \(\vec{w}\) in terms of the new basis, i.e. \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-a-b\\ a+2b\end{smallmatrix}\right)\).

With so many different ways to refer to \(\vec{w}\) now, I’m going to formalize it by letting \(\vec{w}_{old}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) and \(\vec{w}_{new} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}-a-b\\ a+2b\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). For the rest of this solution, \(\vec{w}\) will be reserved for talking about the object itself, independent of any basis. If this sounds redundant, remember that \(\vec{w}_{old}\) and \(\vec{w}_{new}\) are just descriptions of \(\vec{w}\). Think of it as \(\vec{w}\) being an apple, and \(\vec{w}_{old}\) and \(\vec{w}_{new}\) being the words “apple” in English and “蘋果” in Chinese. The two words both refer to the same object, the apple, but neither of them are actually the apple.

To recap, we started with an arbitrary vector \(\vec{w}\)’s coordinate representation in terms of the old basis
(\(\vec{w}_{old}\)) and then did some calculations to obtain \(\vec{w}\)’s coordinate representation in terms of the new basis (\(\vec{w}_{new}\)). Now to get the change-of-basis matrix, we need to figure out how to get from \(\vec{w}_{old}\) to \(\vec{w}_{new}\). This is quite easy, since we can simply use matrix multiplication to decompose \(\vec{w}_{new}\) as follows:

\[\left(\begin{matrix}-a-b\\ a+2b\end{matrix}\right) = \left(\begin{matrix}-1&-1\\1&2\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}a\\ b\end{matrix}\right)\]

Let \(A = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&-1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Then we have that \(\vec{w}_{new} = A\vec{w}_{old}\), so \(A\) must be the change-of-basis matrix. \(\square\).

Well that wasn’t too hard, was it? Except it’s WRONG!!! I looked on Wikipedia afterwards and found that the actual change-of-basis matrix should be the inverse of \(A\), which would be \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-2&-1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). If we call this matrix \(B\), then the relationship we obtain is \(\vec{w}_{old} = B\vec{w}_{new}\).

But doesn’t that seem really weird? Like, now we have a vector expressed in terms of the new basis, and after applying the change-of-basis matrix, we get expression of that vector in the old basis. In other words, it seems like we’re transitioning from the new basis to the old basis, which should be the opposite of what we want. This really confused me, and I’m pretty sure it confused me when I learned about it initially too (which is probably why I couldn’t remember how it worked).

2. A Simpler Problem

I thought that I might be able to get a clearer picture of what’s going on if I made one of the bases the standard basis, since it’s just simpler. So let’s do the problem again, but instead we’ll transition from the standard basis, \(E = \{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right),\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\}\), to \(B_{old}\).

Solution: Let \(\vec{e}_1,\vec{e}_2\) denote the standard basis vectors. We’ll do this exactly the same way, so we’ll first need to find out what the coordinate representations of \(\vec{e}_1,\vec{e}_2\) are in terms of \(B_{old}\); i.e. figure out what \(c_1,c_2,d_1,d_2\) are but for this particular case. This can be done pretty easily with some trial and error since the vectors are simple: \(c_1=1,c_2=0,d_1=-1,d_2=1\) (in other words, with respect to \(B_{old}\), \(\vec{e}_1\) is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) and \(\vec{e}_2\) is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\)). Then for some vector \(\vec{w}\) with standard coordinate representation \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), we have

\[\begin{aligned} \vec{w} &= a\vec{e}_2+b\vec{e}_2 \\ &= a\vec{u}_1+b(-\vec{u}_1+\vec{u}_2) \\ &= (a-b)\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2 \end{aligned}\]

This means that \(\vec{w}_{old} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}a-b\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Then

\[\left(\begin{matrix}a-b\\ b\end{matrix}\right) = \left(\begin{matrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}a\\ b\end{matrix}\right)\]

Taking the inverse of this \(2 \times 2\) matrix, we get that \(C = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) is our change-of-basis matrix. \(\square\).

Interestingly, this inverted matrix didn’t seem weird to me at all, because it encodes the linear transformation which sends \(\spmat{1\\0}\) to \(\spmat{1\\0}\) and \(\spmat{0\\1}\) to \(\spmat{1\\1}\). In other words, \(C\) maps the standard basis vectors onto \(B_{old}\), and thus we change from \(E\) to \(B_{old}\). It’s completely natural that this matrix is the change-of-basis matrix instead of the inverse, since it literally changes the basis!

3. Dealing with Loose Ends

With this, I could understand why the change-of-basis matrix would be the opposite of what I had expected originally, but I still had some questions:

  1. Up until now, I had understood change of basis to be changing how we describe vectors using a different basis. In this framework, the vectors stay still, and it’s the language we use to describe them that changes. But with this linear transformation approach, the vectors are definitely moving. Somehow, the two interpretations converge, but why?
  2. When we start with the standard basis, it’s easy to see that the columns of the change-of-basis matrix are the basis vectors of the new basis (in this case \(B_{old}\)). But in the original problem, the columns of the change-of-basis matrix don’t seem to follow this pattern. Why not?

Recall that \(\vec{u}_1,\vec{u}_2\) denote the basis vectors of \(B_{old}\).

Answer to Question 1: If two different interpretations arise from the same calculation, then there should be some point of ambiguity that allows for that dual interpretation. If we have some vector \(\spmat{a\\ b}\), then the change-of-basis matrix \(C\) acts on it as follows:

\[\pmat{1&1\\0&1}\pmat{a\\ b} = a\pmat{1\\0} + b\pmat{1\\1} = a\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2\]

The point of ambiguity here is that the expression \(\spmat{a\\ b}\) is basis-dependent; i.e. if a basis \(\beta = (\vec{x}_1,\vec{x}_2)\) is established, then \(\spmat{a\\ b}\) actually means \(a\vec{x}_1+b\vec{x}_2\). That vector notation doesn’t mean anything without establishing a basis first, and typically when we use it, we assume that it’s referring to the standard basis. If we interpret \(C\) to be a linear transformation, then \(\spmat{a\\ b}\) is taken to be expressed in the standard basis and therefore \(C\) takes this vector (\(a\vec{e}_1+b\vec{e}_2\)) to \(a\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2\). Since \(\vec{u}_1\) and \(\vec{u}_2\) are both written in terms of the standard basis in the first place, we can substitute in the appropriate expressions for \(\vec{u}_1,\vec{u}_2\) to obtain \((a+b)\vec{e}_1+b\vec{e}_2\). In this interpretation, both the initial and resulting vector are expressed in the standard basis, and thus are legitimately different vectors.

On the other hand if we interpret \(C\) to be as we originally interpreted it, then \(\spmat{a\\ b}\) actually means \(a\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2\). Unlike in the linear transformation interpretation, the calculation now takes \(a\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2\) to \(a\spmat{1\\0}+b\spmat{1\\1}\). But of course, \(\spmat{1\\0}\) is the representation of \(\vec{u}_1\) in the standard basis and \(\spmat{1\\1}\) is the representation of \(\vec{u}_2\) in the standard basis, so these two vectors are actually the same object, just represented in terms of different bases. Here, we started with a vector expressed in \(B_{old}\) and ended up with the same vector expressed in the standard basis.

I spent a long time trying to reconcile these two interpretations. I wanted an explicit connection that showed that changing the basis like in the second interpretation was somehow the same action as the linear transformation. But you can’t really get around the fact that the vectors move in one interpretation and don’t move in the other. The reality is that the abstract nature of calculations like these open themselves to different interpretations which aren’t always strongly connected. Still though, I wanted a stronger intuition, instead of just being two ways of viewing the same calculation.

The One Dimensional Case: Imagine you have 3 meters of thread, and you want to know how many centimeters of thread you have. You might say that since there are 100cm in a meter, we would calculate:

\[(100\textrm{cm/m})(3\textrm{m}) = 300\textrm{cm}\]

Here we view 300cm and 3m as the same quantity, we’re just converting units. This is analogous to the “change of basis” interpretation. Alternatively, you might be a psycopath and say that since there are 100cm in a meter, then we simply need to transform every centimeter into 100cm by scaling by 100. Accordingly, 3cm is scaled as follows:

\[100(3\textrm{cm}) = 3(100\cdot 1\textrm{cm}) = 3(100\textrm{cm}) = 300\textrm{cm}\]

Here our world is measured in terms of 1cm, and then to get our answer we change the entire measurement system from counting in units of 1cm to units of 100cm. We don’t start with 3 meters and convert that into centimeters. Instead, that’s kind of baked into this new measurement system that counts in units of 100cm. This is analogous to the linear transformation interpretation. Of course, the two calculations are just multiplying 3 by 100.

The difference here is pretty subtle, and it was quite hard for me to understand where exactly the linear transformation approach differed from just how I typically think about unit conversion. But it then dawned on me that this was exactly what I was looking for: a strong intuition that connected the two distinctly different approaches. With this, the first question is answered.

Answer to Question 2: The columns of the change-of-basis matrix \(B\) do follow the same pattern, but it just doesn’t look like it since we originally expressed the vectors in terms of the standard basis. Taking the matrix \(C\) from the simplified problem, the \(i\)th column is \(\vec{u}_i\) relative to the standard basis (old basis in this case). Therefore, the \(i\)th column of the matrix \(B\) should be \(\vec{v}_i\) relative to \(B_{old}\). Its easy to verify that this is the case:

\[\begin{aligned} -2\vec{u}_1+1\vec{u}_2 &= -2\pmat{1\\0} + 1\pmat{1\\1} \\ &= \pmat{-1\\1} = \vec{v}_1 \\ -1\vec{u}_1+1\vec{u}_2 &= -1\pmat{1\\0}+1\pmat{1\\1} \\ &= \pmat{0\\1} = \vec{v}_2 \end{aligned}\]

Thus, relative to \(B_{old}\), \(\vec{v}_1 = \spmat{-2\\1}\) and \(\vec{v}_2 = \spmat{-1\\1}\) as desired. Hence Question 2 has been answered.

4. Maybe the Real Change-of-Basis Matrix was the Friends We Made Along the Way

So where did all that leave me? What I now knew was that:

  1. The proper change-of-basis matrix was the inverse of what I had initially thought it should be.
  2. This inverted matrix makes sense because of how it acts on the basis vectors when thought of as a linear transformation.
  3. This linear transformation interpretation is strongly connected to the change of basis interpretation; they are two different ways to achieve the same result of “unit conversion”.
  4. I can calculate the change-of-basis matrix easily by first calculating what the new basis vectors are relative to the old basis. Then the columns of the change-of-basis matrix are just these resulting coordinate vectors.

But this didn’t tell me why my original matrix wasn’t the right one. After all, that matrix did take vectors expressed in the old basis to their coordinates relative to the new basis. How annoying!

Just kidding, I didn’t really care about that at all, since that’s just something that happens a lot. The two matrices are inverses, so it doesn’t really matter which one you pick to be the change-of-basis matrix. You can do everything you can do with one matrix with the other. You’d just have to flip some stuff around to make it equivalent. My guess is that the action on the basis vectors themselves seemed more straightforward, so that’s why that one was chosen for the definition. Unfortunately, that makes some things inconvenient, like the aforementioned relation \(\vec{w}_{old} = B\vec{w}_{new}\). Wikipedia even comments that this is confusing, but with what I’ve covered in this post, I definitely feel a lot better about it, so I’m fine with that. You can’t win ‘em all, I guess.
